kurals.tamil:
செல்லிடத்துக் காப்பான் சினங்காப்பான் அல்லிடத்துக்
காக்கின்என் காவாக்கா லென்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sellidaththuk kaappaan sinangaappaan allidaththuk
Kaakkin en kaavaakkaal en.
kurals.meaning: The one who truly restrains anger is the one who holds it back where it could actually take effect and do harm. Where anger has no power to act anyway, what difference does it make whether you hold it back or not?
kurals.elementary: Imagine a big kid who could easily push a small kid, but chooses not to. That is real self-control. If a small kid can't push a big kid anyway, 'not pushing' isn't really a choice. This kural says being calm only counts when you really could have hurt someone and you don't.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter by redefining the virtue itself: restraint of anger (sinam kaaththal) is morally meaningful only where one has the power (sellidam, literally 'the place where it goes through') to make the anger effective. Classical commentators such as Parimelazhagar read sellidam as the case of anger toward those weaker than oneself, where retaliation would succeed; restraint toward the stronger is mere prudence or fear. The couplet thus locates virtue in the gap between capacity and action, anticipating the Aristotelian and Stoic view that a virtue is shown only where its opposite is genuinely available. The rhetorical question of the second line ('what if he guards it, what if he does not?') dismisses 'restraint' that costs nothing as morally empty.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata's Adi Parva, the sage Vasishtha, who possessed immense spiritual power, suffered the killing of his hundred sons through the machinations tied to his rival Vishvamitra, yet he did not use that power to destroy Vishvamitra; instead he bore his grief without retaliation.
hinduism.explanation: Vasishtha is the classic Indian image of a sage who could have annihilated his enemy but chose not to unleash his wrath.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the kural's 'restraint where anger would take effect': Vasishtha's patience matters because his power to punish was real.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Chaitraratha Parva, the Vasishtha–Vishvamitra episode)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match (power plus restraint). Paraphrase of a narrative episode; details vary across retellings and the sons' deaths are attributed to the cursed king Kalmashapada acting at Vishvamitra's instigation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?”
christianity.explanation: At his arrest, Jesus tells Peter to put away his sword and points out that he could summon overwhelming force, yet he chooses not to.
christianity.tie_back: Like the kural, the restraint is meaningful precisely because the power to retaliate is fully available.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV. The verse is about non-retaliation with power in hand rather than anger as an emotion, but the structure matches the kural closely.

islam.quote_or_event: “If anyone suppresses anger when he is in a position to give vent to it, Allah, the Exalted, will call him on the Day of Resurrection over the heads of all creatures...”
islam.explanation: The Prophet singles out for special honour the person who swallows anger at the very moment he is able to act on it.
islam.tie_back: Near one-to-one with the kural: the merit lies in restraining anger 'when in a position to give vent to it', which is exactly Valluvar's sellidam.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4777 (graded hasan by al-Albani)
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim from sunnah.com English; the condition 'when he is in a position to give vent to it' mirrors the kural almost exactly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city’ (Proverbs 16:32).”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines strength: real might is mastery over one's own impulses, and he grounds this in the verse praising the one who is slow to anger.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say that the real test of power is turning it inward to master one's own anger rather than outward against others.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim. Shares the 'true strength is restraint' idea but lacks the kural's specific contrast between effective and ineffective anger.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who checks rising anger as a charioteer checks a rolling chariot, him I call a true charioteer. Others only hold the reins.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares controlling anger to reining in a chariot already in motion; merely holding the reins when nothing is moving is not mastery.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the kural, only restraint at the moment of real momentum counts; 'others only hold the reins' parallels Valluvar's dismissal of costless restraint.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verbatim. Very close structural parallel between genuine restraint and mere appearance of control.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He stayed his hand on the silver hilt of his sword, and thrust it back into the scabbard as Minerva bade him.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Insulted by Agamemnon, Achilles is already drawing his sword to kill him when Athena (Minerva) intervenes and he sheathes it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A picture of anger checked at the moment it could take effect, though in Homer the restraint comes from a goddess rather than from Achilles' own virtue.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verbatim Butler. Good image of restraint at the point of action, but the restraint is divinely imposed and Achilles keeps raging verbally.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Am I more powerful than Philip? yet he allowed a man to curse him with impunity. Have I more authority in my own house than the Emperor Augustus possessed throughout the world?”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca advises that whenever we are provoked we should recall rulers who had total power to punish yet chose to let insults pass.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca, like Valluvar, measures self-control by what one could do with one's power and refrains from doing.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira), Book III (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1900)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim from the Wikisource Stewart translation. Strong match on restraint by the powerful.

kurals.tamil:
செல்லா இடத்துச் சினந்தீது செல்லிடத்தும்
இல்அதனின் தீய பிற.
kurals.transliteration:
Sellaa idaththuch sinandheedhu sellidaththum
Il adhanin theeya pira.
kurals.meaning: Anger where it cannot take effect (against those stronger than you) is harmful to yourself. And where it can take effect (against those weaker than you), there is nothing more evil than it.
kurals.elementary: If you get angry at a much bigger kid, you will probably get hurt. If you get angry at a much smaller kid, you might hurt them, and that is even worse. So anger is bad either way: it hurts you, or it makes you hurt someone who can't fight back.
kurals.university: This couplet completes the argument of 301 by closing every escape route: anger is bad where it is ineffective (sellaa idam, anger toward the powerful, which rebounds on oneself) and worst of all where it is effective (sellidam, anger toward the weak, which inflicts real injury). Mu. Varadarasanar's gloss makes the two cases explicit as 'stronger' and 'weaker' persons. The ethical weight falls on the second line: power over others magnifies the moral gravity of anger rather than licensing it. The structure anticipates modern concerns about abuse of authority in households, workplaces, and states, where anger combined with power becomes cruelty.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, the ascetic Kaushika burns a crane to death with an angry glance after it soils him; later, when a devoted housewife keeps him waiting, his anger has no effect on her, and she rebukes him with the words that she is not a crane, directing him to learn true dharma from a humble meat-seller.
hinduism.explanation: Kaushika's anger kills a helpless bird but is powerless against a righteous woman, and the story treats both as evidence of his spiritual failure.
hinduism.tie_back: The two halves of the kural in narrative form: anger at the weak is destructive evil, and anger at the strong is futile and humiliating.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Markandeya-Samasya Parva, the tale of Kaushika, the devoted wife, and the Dharmavyadha)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; the pairing of effective and ineffective anger matches the kural unusually well.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And, ye masters, do the same things unto them, forbearing threatening: knowing that your Master also is in heaven; neither is there respect of persons with him.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells those who hold power over servants to give up threats, reminding them that they themselves answer to a higher Master.
christianity.tie_back: Matches the kural's second line: where you have power over the weak, harsh anger and threats are especially wrong.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV. Addresses anger or threat toward subordinates; does not address the 'anger at the stronger' half.

islam.quote_or_event: “Bear in mind, Abu Mas'ud; verily Allah has more dominance upon you than you have upon your slave.”
islam.explanation: Abu Mas'ud was whipping his slave in intense anger when the Prophet stopped him with this reminder; he dropped the whip and vowed never to beat a servant again.
islam.tie_back: Directly illustrates the kural's warning that anger toward those under your power is the worst evil, and that you yourself stand under a greater power.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim sunnah.com English. Excellent match for anger against the weak; implicit on anger against the strong.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A person should never impose excessive fear upon the members of his household, as the husband of the concubine of Gibeah imposed excessive fear upon her and this ultimately caused the downfall of many tens of thousands of Jews.”
judaism.explanation: Rav Hisda warns that intimidating those under your authority at home can spiral into catastrophe, citing the story in Judges 19–20.
judaism.tie_back: Like the kural, the Talmud singles out anger and intimidation directed at dependents as especially destructive.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 6b (William Davidson/Koren-Steinsaltz trans., via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim Sefaria English (bold markup removed). About domestic intimidation rooted in anger; fits the 'where anger is effective' half.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Angered & displeased, she grabbed hold of a rolling pin and gave her a whack over the head, cutting it open.”
buddhism.explanation: Lady Vedehika was famed for gentleness, but her slave Kali tested her; when provoked, the mistress struck her only slave, and her reputation became 'vicious' and 'violent'.
buddhism.tie_back: The story shows that anger vented on someone powerless is the true test of character and the worst of evils, just as the kural says.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 21, Kakacupama Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verbatim. Also echoes 301: Vedehika's calm was only apparent while her anger had no occasion.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “A plain man cannot stand against the anger of a king, who if he swallow his displeasure now, will yet nurse revenge till he has wreaked it.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The seer Calchas fears Agamemnon's anger, and indeed Agamemnon's harsh treatment of the helpless priest Chryses brings a plague on the army, while his quarrel with the stronger Achilles brings disaster on the Greeks.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Iliad Book 1 shows both halves: anger at the powerless (Chryses) is cruelty, and anger at the powerful (Achilles) rebounds on oneself.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verbatim Butler. Thematic rather than doctrinal match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Why should I make my slave atone by stripes and manacles for having answered me too loudly or having put on a stubborn look, or muttered something which I did not catch? Who am I, that it should be a crime to shock my ears?”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues against anger at dependents, and elsewhere in the same book praises Augustus for stopping Vedius Pollio from feeding a slave to lampreys over a broken cup.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca, like the kural, finds anger most shameful where one has total power over its victim.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira), Book III (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1900)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim Stewart translation (Wikisource). Close match for anger toward the weak.

kurals.tamil:
மறத்தல் வெகுளியை யார்மாட்டும் தீய
பிறத்தல் அதனான் வரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Maraththal vekuliyai yaarmaattum theeya
Piraththal adhanaan varum.
kurals.meaning: Let go of anger toward anyone at all, and forget it, for every kind of evil is born from anger.
kurals.elementary: Anger is like a seed that grows weeds. If you keep it, bad things grow out of it: mean words, fights, broken friendships. So the kural says: let go of anger, no matter who made you angry.
kurals.university: The verb maraththal ('forgetting', 'letting go') is significant: Valluvar does not ask merely for suppression but for the anger to be dropped from memory, since resentment that is stored continues to generate harm. Yaarmaattum ('toward anyone whatsoever') universalises the precept, removing the distinctions of power drawn in 301 and 302. The second line offers a causal claim: evils (theeya) are 'born' (piraththal) from anger, making it a root vice rather than one fault among many. This genealogical view of anger as a source of other wrongs parallels the Buddhist treatment of dosa as one of the three roots of unwholesome action and the Gita's chain from desire to anger to ruin.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There are three gates leading to this hell – lust, anger and greed. Every sane man should give these up, for they lead to the degradation of the soul.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna names anger as one of three gateways to ruin and commands that it be abandoned.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the kural, the Gita calls for giving anger up entirely because destruction flows from it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verbatim vedabase. Anger as a source of evil, to be relinquished.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath: Neither give place to the devil.”
christianity.explanation: Paul allows that anger may arise but insists it not be kept overnight, since lingering wrath gives the devil a foothold.
christianity.tie_back: Parallels the kural's 'forget anger': do not hold on to it, because harm grows from it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV. Close on releasing anger quickly; Paul tolerates momentary anger where the kural urges total release.

islam.quote_or_event: “A man said to the Prophet, ‘Advise me!’ The Prophet said, ‘Do not become angry.’ The man asked (the same) again and again, and the Prophet said in each case, ‘Do not become angry.’”
islam.explanation: Asked for comprehensive advice, the Prophet gives a single repeated instruction to avoid anger.
islam.tie_back: Like the kural, this treats giving up anger as a master key, since so much wrongdoing springs from it.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim sunnah.com English (punctuation lightly normalised). Universal prohibition matches 'toward anyone'.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids both revenge and holding a grudge, pairing this with the command to love one's neighbour.
judaism.tie_back: The ban on 'bearing a grudge' is close to the kural's 'forget anger'; both demand that resentment be released, not stored.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim JPS 1917 via Sefaria. Strong match on letting go of resentment; no explicit claim that evils spring from anger.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “‘He abused me, he struck me, he overpowered me, he robbed me.’ Those who do not harbor such thoughts still their hatred.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that rehearsing grievances keeps hatred alive, while letting them go ends it.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly the kural's own advice: forgetting the offence is how anger, and the evils it breeds, are ended.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verbatim. Very close to maraththal (forgetting) as the cure.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Western literature's first epic opens by naming its subject as one man's wrath and the endless suffering it caused.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Homer and Valluvar agree that anger is a fountain of evils; the Iliad is effectively a narrative proof of the kural's second line.
greek_mythology.source: Homer, Iliad, Book 1, opening lines (trans. Samuel Butler)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verbatim Butler. Strong on 'evils born of anger'; Homer does not prescribe forgetting it.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Next, if you choose to view its results and the mischief that it does, no plague has cost the human race more dear.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca lists the slaughters, poisonings, and ruined cities that anger has produced.
philosophy.tie_back: A direct philosophical counterpart to 'evils are born of anger'.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira), Book I (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1900)

kurals.tamil:
நகையும் உவகையும் கொல்லும் சினத்தின்
பகையும் உளவோ பிற.
kurals.transliteration:
Nagaiyum uvagaiyum kollum sinaththin
Pagaiyum ulavo pira.
kurals.meaning: Anger kills both the smile on the face and the joy in the heart. Is there any enemy greater than that?
kurals.elementary: When you are really angry, you can't laugh and you can't feel happy. It's like a thief that steals your smile. The kural asks: what enemy could be worse than one that takes away all your happiness?
kurals.university: Valluvar pairs nagai (laughter, the outward cheerfulness of the face) with uvagai (inner delight), a pairing the commentators render as 'face-blossoming and heart-blossoming'. Anger 'kills' both, so the damage is not only social but inward. The rhetorical question reframes anger as a pagai (enemy) that lives within, which is more dangerous than any external foe because it cannot be escaped. The idea of anger as an internal enemy runs through Indian thought (the 'six inner enemies', including krodha) and has close parallels in the Buddhist teaching that an angry person does to himself what an enemy would wish on him.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material mode of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna identifies desire turned into wrath as the 'all-devouring' enemy that must be known and conquered.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the kural, the Gita names anger as the greatest enemy, one that consumes a person from within.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verbatim vedabase. The verse centres on lust (kama) turning into wrath (krodha); the 'enemy' framing matches the kural closely.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife ... But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,”
christianity.explanation: Paul sets wrath among the 'works of the flesh' and sets joy and peace among the fruits of the Spirit.
christianity.tie_back: The contrast shows wrath and joy as opposites, as in the kural, where anger kills joy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV (abridged with ellipsis). The link between wrath and joy is implied by contrast, not stated.

islam.quote_or_event: “Anger is an ember in the heart of the son of Adam, as you see it in the redness of his eyes and the bulge of his jugular veins. So whoever senses something from that, then let him cling to the ground.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet describes anger as a burning coal that visibly disfigures the face and body.
islam.tie_back: Like the kural, this shows anger taking over the face and heart, replacing calm cheer with burning.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim sunnah.com English. LOW-CONFIDENCE SOURCE: this narration is graded weak (da'if); good thematic fit but should not be presented as authoritative hadith.

judaism.quote_or_event: When God accepted Abel's offering and not his, Cain became very angry and his face fell; God asked him why he was angry and why his face had fallen, warning that sin was crouching at the door.
judaism.explanation: In the Torah's first account of anger, the emotion shows immediately on Cain's face and leads him to kill his brother.
judaism.tie_back: Cain's 'fallen countenance' is the kural's lost smile: anger strips the face of light before it does any other harm.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase (JPS 1917 wording not re-checked this session because of a fetch rate limit). Strong image of anger destroying the face's cheer.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Having killed anger you sleep in ease. Having killed anger you do not grieve. The noble ones praise the slaying of anger — with its honeyed crest & poison root —”
buddhism.explanation: Asked what one thing should be killed, the Buddha answers: anger, because killing it brings ease and ends grief.
buddhism.tie_back: The reverse of the kural: anger kills joy, and killing anger restores it.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 1.71, Ghatva Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verbatim (line breaks collapsed). Joy and anger presented as mutually exclusive, as in the kural.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But Achilles abode at his ships and nursed his anger. He went not to the honourable assembly, and sallied not forth to fight, but gnawed at his own heart, pining for battle and the war-cry.”
greek_mythology.explanation: After his quarrel, Achilles withdraws from everything he loves and consumes himself with resentment.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles 'gnawing at his own heart' is anger killing the angry man's own joy, as the kural says.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verbatim Butler. Good dramatic match for anger as a self-consuming enemy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Eighth, consider how much more pain is brought on us by the anger and vexation caused by such acts than by the acts themselves, at which we are angry and vexed.”
philosophy.explanation: Among his rules for handling offence, Marcus observes that our own anger hurts us more than the offence did.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the kural, Marcus treats anger as the real enemy of our peace of mind, worse than any outside wrong.

kurals.tamil:
தன்னைத்தான் காக்கின் சினங்காக்க காவாக்கால்
தன்னையே கொல்லுஞ் சினம்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thannaiththaan kaakkin sinangaakka kaavaakkaal
Thannaiye kollum sinam.
kurals.meaning: If you want to protect yourself, guard against anger. If you do not guard against it, anger will destroy you yourself.
kurals.elementary: Anger is like a fire you carry in your own pocket. If you don't put it out, it burns you first. So the best way to keep yourself safe is to keep anger away.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on the reflexive thannai ('oneself'), which frames it: the whole argument is about self-preservation, not the protection of others. Valluvar's point is strategic as much as moral: anger, left unguarded, turns back on its owner, destroying health, judgment, reputation, and eventually life. The repetition of kaa ('guard') across both lines makes guarding anger identical with guarding the self. This self-interested argument against anger complements the altruistic ones elsewhere in the chapter and matches Stoic and Buddhist analyses that anger harms its owner before its target.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “From anger, complete delusion arises, and from delusion bewilderment of memory. When memory is bewildered, intelligence is lost, and when intelligence is lost one falls down again into the material pool.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna traces a chain of self-destruction: anger leads to delusion, loss of memory, and loss of intelligence, ending in ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita's final step, 'praṇaśyati' ('one perishes'), is the kural's 'anger will kill you'.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verbatim vedabase. Near one-to-one: unguarded anger destroys the angry person.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For wrath killeth the foolish man, and envy slayeth the silly one.”
christianity.explanation: Eliphaz, speaking in Job, states a proverb that wrath is fatal to the one who harbours it.
christianity.tie_back: Almost a restatement of the kural's second line: anger kills its own owner.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV. Note that Job's friends' speeches are not always endorsed by the book, but this proverb is widely cited as wisdom.

islam.quote_or_event: “The strong is not the one who overcomes the people by his strength, but the strong is the one who controls himself while in anger.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet redefines strength as self-control at the moment of anger.
islam.tie_back: Like the kural, the emphasis is on guarding oneself (yamliku nafsahu, 'controls himself') against one's own anger.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim sunnah.com English. Matches 'guard yourself'; the hadith does not state the self-destruction consequence.

judaism.quote_or_event: At Meribah, Moses, angered by the people, addressed them as 'rebels' and struck the rock instead of speaking to it; as a result God decreed that he would not bring Israel into the Promised Land.
judaism.explanation: Jewish tradition (for example Maimonides in his Eight Chapters) identifies Moses' failing here as anger, which cost the greatest prophet his life's goal.
judaism.tie_back: Even for Moses, failing to guard against anger turned it against himself, as the kural warns.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Interpretation of Moses' sin as anger is Maimonides' reading; other commentators give different reasons.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like oneself, all beings hold themselves most dear, yet an angry person, deranged, can kill himself in many ways: with a sword, taking poison, hanging himself by a rope in a mountain glen.”
buddhism.explanation: The verses of the Kodhana Sutta describe how anger can drive a person to destroy even himself.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost literally the kural's 'anger will kill you yourself'.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.60, Kodhana Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verbatim (verse line breaks collapsed). Near one-to-one.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Denied the armour of the dead Achilles, Ajax sets out in rage to kill the Greek commanders; Athena drives him mad so that he slaughters livestock instead, and on waking in shame he falls on his own sword.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sophocles' tragedy shows unchecked wrath ending in the self-destruction of the greatest warrior after Achilles.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A literal enactment of 'if you do not guard against anger, it will kill you'.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the plot; strong narrative match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...careless of itself provided it hurts another, rushing upon the very point of the sword, and greedy for revenge even when it drags the avenger to ruin with itself.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca opens De Ira by describing anger as a passion that will wreck its owner so long as it can harm someone else.
philosophy.tie_back: Seneca's 'drags the avenger to ruin with itself' is the kural's point exactly.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira), Book I.1 (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1900)

kurals.tamil:
சினமென்னும் சேர்ந்தாரைக் கொல்லி இனமென்னும்
ஏமப் புணையைச் சுடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sinamennum serndhaaraik kolli inamennum
Emap punaiyaich sudum.
kurals.meaning: Anger is a fire that kills whoever comes near it, and it burns up even the raft of kinsmen and friends that would carry a person safely through life.
kurals.elementary: Think of your family and friends as a raft that keeps you floating in a big river. Anger is like a fire on that raft. If you let it burn, it destroys the very thing that keeps you safe.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a compound metaphor. Sinam is called serndhaaraik kolli, 'the killer of those who come close', a traditional kenning for fire, which destroys whatever touches it. Inam, one's kin and circle of friends, is called an emap punai, a 'safe raft' that carries one across the dangerous sea of life. Anger, being fire, burns the very raft that was meant to save its owner: it isolates the angry person by consuming the relationships that sustain them. Valluvar thus extends the self-harm argument of 305 to its social dimension.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After setting Lanka ablaze in fury, Hanuman is struck with horror that his fire may have burned Sita herself; he reproaches his own anger and praises those great souls who, by their wisdom, quench anger as it rises, as fire is put out with water.
hinduism.explanation: Hanuman's rage, turned into literal fire, threatens the very person he came to save.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost exactly the kural's image: anger is a fire that burns what we hold dear, the raft that was meant to save us.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the fire and water image appears in Hanuman's lament. Sarga numbering follows the critical/common Southern recension and may differ between editions.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns a quarrelling community that mutual hostility will consume them all.
christianity.tie_back: Like the kural, anger among companions destroys the community that sustains each member.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV. Matches the social-destruction theme; lacks the fire imagery.

islam.quote_or_event: “Anger comes from the devil, the devil was created of fire, and fire is extinguished only with water; so when one of you becomes angry, he should perform ablution.”
islam.explanation: This narration describes anger as a fire and prescribes water (ablution) to put it out.
islam.tie_back: Shares the kural's core metaphor of anger as a consuming fire.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 4784 (graded da'if by al-Albani)
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim sunnah.com English. LOW-CONFIDENCE SOURCE: graded weak (da'if). Fire image matches, but the kinship dimension is absent.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce, And their wrath, for it was cruel; I will divide them in Jacob, And scatter them in Israel.”
judaism.explanation: On his deathbed Jacob condemns the violent anger of his sons Simeon and Levi and foretells that their tribes will be scattered.
judaism.tie_back: The anger of Simeon and Levi ends up breaking apart their own tribes: the kural's burning of the 'raft of kin'.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim JPS 1917 via Sefaria. Strong match on anger destroying one's own kin-group.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Now, when a person is angry — overcome with anger, oppressed with anger — his friends, companions, & relatives will avoid him from afar, all because he is overcome with anger.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the seven things an enemy wishes on an enemy is friendlessness, and anger brings it about.
buddhism.tie_back: Direct parallel: anger drives away the kin and friends who form one's safe raft.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 7.60, Kodhana Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Consumed by rage at Jason's betrayal, Medea kills their own children to wound him, destroying her family and her own future.
greek_mythology.explanation: Euripides' Medea is the Greek archetype of anger turning against the angry person's own kin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Medea's fury burns the very family that bound her life together, as the kural's fire burns the raft of kin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the plot; her anger is provoked by real injustice, which the kural's generalisation does not address.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Such people are most troublesome to themselves and to their dearest friends.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle, describing the sulky temperament that nurses anger for a long time, notes that it torments both the person and those closest to him.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the kural, Aristotle sees lasting anger damaging one's closest relationships as well as oneself.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.5 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim Ross (MIT Classics). Aristotle, unlike Valluvar, allows anger 'at the right things'; the match is on the harm of excessive anger.

kurals.tamil:
சினத்தைப் பொருளென்று கொண்டவன் கேடு
நிலத்தறைந்தான் கைபிழையா தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Sinaththaip porulendru kondavan kedu
Nilaththaraindhaan kai pizhaiyaadhatru.
kurals.meaning: Ruin will surely come to the person who treats anger as something valuable, just as surely as the hand of a person who strikes the ground cannot escape being hurt.
kurals.elementary: If you slap the floor as hard as you can, the floor doesn't feel anything, but your hand really hurts. Using anger as your 'power' is the same: the person who uses it gets hurt the most.
kurals.university: The target here is a specific attitude: treating anger as porul, a thing of worth or a useful tool, whether as a mark of strength, a way to command respect, or a means of getting results. The simile of striking the ground (nilaththu araindhaan) is precise: the ground is unharmed while the striker's hand is certain to be injured, so anger's force rebounds on its user. Kai pizhaiyaadhu ('the hand does not escape') stresses certainty, not mere probability. The couplet enters a long-running debate, found in Aristotle and Seneca, about whether anger is a useful servant of virtue; Valluvar sides firmly with those who deny it any value.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The sage Durvasa, enraged that King Ambarisha broke his fast before Durvasa returned, creates a fiery demon to kill the king; Vishnu's discus destroys the demon and then pursues Durvasa through all the worlds until he humbly seeks the forgiveness of the very king he attacked.
hinduism.explanation: Durvasa, famous for wielding anger as power, finds his own wrath turned back upon himself.
hinduism.tie_back: A narrative version of the struck ground: the anger he valued as a weapon rebounds on its user.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; strong 'boomerang' match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein: and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb states that harm aimed at others returns to its author.
christianity.tie_back: The same rebound logic as the kural's hand striking the ground.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV. General retribution principle rather than a statement about anger specifically.

islam.quote_or_event: “...but the evil plot does not encompass except its own people.”
islam.explanation: The Quran states that malicious scheming ultimately surrounds and ruins those who devise it.
islam.tie_back: Like the kural, harm that springs from hostility returns upon its originator.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim excerpt. Concerns evil plotting and arrogance rather than anger per se; next-best match.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry; For anger resteth in the bosom of fools.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet warns against quick anger, saying it 'rests' or is cherished in the bosom of fools.
judaism.tie_back: The fool who keeps anger in his bosom is the one who 'takes anger as a treasure' in the kural, and both texts expect his undoing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim JPS 1917 via Sefaria. Matches the 'cherishing anger' half; the rebound image is absent.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Like fine dust thrown against the wind, evil falls back upon that fool who offends an inoffensive, pure and guiltless man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares harming the innocent to throwing dust into the wind, where it blows back into the thrower's face.
buddhism.tie_back: A near-identical physical image to the hand striking the ground: the force returns to its source.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verbatim. Excellent match on the rebound image.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Achilles nurses his wrath against Agamemnon as a matter of honour and refuses to fight; the result is the death of his dearest friend Patroclus, after which he bitterly curses strife and anger.
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles treats his anger as something precious, a defence of his honour, and it destroys what he loved most.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The anger he valued rebounds on him, as the hand striking the earth cannot escape pain.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; Book 18 lament not quoted because the exact Butler wording was not re-verified this session.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...and very like a falling rock which breaks itself to pieces upon the very thing which it crushes.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca's opening description of anger compares it to a falling rock that shatters on what it hits; later he rejects Aristotle's view that anger is a useful 'weapon' for virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: Both the image (force that shatters its source) and the argument (anger has no real value) match the kural.
philosophy.source: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira), Book I.1 (trans. Aubrey Stewart, 1900)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim Stewart translation (Wikisource). Very close image and argument.

kurals.tamil:
இணர்எரி தோய்வன்ன இன்னா செயினும்
புணரின் வெகுளாமை நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Inar eri thoivanna innaa seyinum
Punarin vekulaamai nandru.
kurals.meaning: Even if someone does you harm as painful as being plunged into a blazing fire, it is good, if you possibly can, to refrain from anger toward them.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes people are so mean it feels like being burned. The kural says: even then, if you can, try not to become angry back. It is really hard, but it is the best and bravest thing to do.
kurals.university: This is the chapter's high-water mark of demand: inar eri, a fire of many clustered flames, is the image of the worst possible injury. The concessive punarin ('if it is possible', or in some readings 'if the offender seeks reconciliation') is realistic, acknowledging that non-anger in such extremity may exceed ordinary capacity, but it does not lower the ideal. Kalaignar's gloss takes punarin as the wrongdoer returning to seek friendship, making the couplet about accepting reconciliation without resentment. Either way, the teaching approaches the most radical ethics of non-retaliation found across traditions.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The boy Prahlada is subjected by his own father, Hiranyakashipu, to repeated attempts on his life, including poison, serpents, being thrown from heights, and fire, yet he keeps his devotion and shows no hatred toward his father.
hinduism.explanation: Prahlada becomes the Puranic model of a person who suffers extreme cruelty without answering in anger.
hinduism.tie_back: A living example of the kural's ideal: meeting fire-like torment without wrath.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. The popular Holika fire episode comes from later tradition; the Bhagavata lists a range of torments. Prahlada's lack of anger is emphasised in the Purana's portrayal.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.”
christianity.explanation: On the cross, in extreme agony, Jesus prays for those who are crucifying him.
christianity.tie_back: The fullest Christian expression of the kural's ideal: no anger even under torment 'like fire'.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV (first clause). Very strong match.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Quran instructs believers to answer harm with good, promising that this can turn an enemy into a close friend.
islam.tie_back: Matches both the non-anger ideal and Kalaignar's reading of punarin as reconciliation with the offender.

judaism.quote_or_event: “About those who are insulted and do not insult, who hear their shame and do not respond, who act out of love and are joyful in suffering, the verse says: ‘And they that love Him are as the sun going forth in its might’ (Judges 5:31).”
judaism.explanation: The Sages praise those who absorb humiliation without striking back, comparing them to the rising sun in its strength.
judaism.tie_back: Like the kural, the Talmud treats not answering injury with anger as a sign of greatness.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 88b (William Davidson/Koren-Steinsaltz trans., via Sefaria)

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, even if bandits were to carve you up savagely, limb by limb, with a two-handled saw, he among you who let his heart get angered even at that would not be doing my bidding.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Simile of the Saw, the Buddha sets the most extreme standard of non-anger imaginable.
buddhism.tie_back: Near one-to-one with the kural's 'even if they plunge you into fire', and even stricter, since it drops the 'if possible' qualification.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 21, Kakacupama Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Priam goes alone to the tent of Achilles, who has killed his son Hector and defiled his body, and kisses the hands of his son's killer to beg for the corpse; Achilles, moved, puts aside his wrath and returns the body.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad ends not with victory but with two enemies setting aside anger in the face of unbearable loss.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Priam's restraint before the man who burned his life to ashes reflects the kural's ideal of non-anger after the worst injury.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Priam's motive is love for his son rather than a principle of non-anger.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.”
philosophy.explanation: In prison awaiting execution, Socrates holds that retaliation is never just, no matter how much one has suffered.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates' 'whatever evil we may have suffered' is the Greek counterpart of the kural's 'even if they harm you like fire'.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim Jowett (MIT Classics). Concerns retaliation (action) more than anger (emotion).

kurals.tamil:
உள்ளிய தெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும் உள்ளத்தால்
உள்ளான் வெகுளி எனின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ulliyadhellaam udaneydhum ullaththaal
Ullaan vekuli enin.
kurals.meaning: If a person never lets even the thought of anger enter the mind, he will attain at once everything he sets his heart on.
kurals.elementary: When your mind isn't full of angry thoughts, it has lots of room for good ideas and plans. People also like to help calm, kind people. So a mind without anger can reach its goals much more easily.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on the root ul- ('to think', 'the mind'): ulliyadhu ('what one has thought of'), ullaththaal ('in the mind'), and ullaan ('does not think of'). Valluvar sets the standard at the level of thought itself: it is not enough to avoid angry acts or words; one must not entertain (ullaan) anger inwardly. The promised reward, attaining all one intends 'at once' (udan), is striking, and commentators variously read it as worldly success (a clear mind and goodwill from others) or spiritual attainment. The couplet thus links inner purity from anger to efficacy in the world, a pattern also found in the Gita's promise of liberation for those free of desire and anger.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Those who are free from anger and all material desires, who are self-realized, self-disciplined and constantly endeavoring for perfection, are assured of liberation in the Supreme in the very near future.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna promises that freedom from anger and desire brings the highest goal near at hand.
hinduism.tie_back: Close to the kural: the one free of anger in mind attains what is sought, and attains it soon ('abhitaḥ', 'near at hand', like Valluvar's 'udan', 'at once').
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verbatim vedabase. The Gita's reward is spiritual liberation, while the kural's may be read more broadly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.”
christianity.explanation: In the Beatitudes, Jesus promises the whole earth to the meek, those gentle and slow to anger.
christianity.tie_back: Like the kural, the non-angry are promised a surprisingly large reward.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV. 'Meek' includes but is broader than 'free of anger'.

islam.quote_or_event: “And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a garden as wide as the heavens and earth, prepared for the righteous ... who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allah loves the doers of good;”
islam.explanation: The Quran lists restraining anger and pardoning others among the qualities of those promised a vast paradise.
islam.tie_back: Like the kural, freedom from anger is tied directly to receiving the greatest reward.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim, abridged with ellipsis. 'Restrain anger' (al-kazimin al-ghayz) is suppression rather than never thinking of it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “With regard to whoever forgoes his reckonings with others for injustices done to him, the heavenly court in turn forgoes punishment for all his sins.”
judaism.explanation: Rava teaches that one who lets go of grievances receives complete forgiveness; the passage then tells of Rav Huna recovering from near-death because he never insisted on his rights.
judaism.tie_back: Like the kural, the person who does not hold anger in mind receives an extraordinary, all-encompassing reward.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 17a (William Davidson/Koren-Steinsaltz trans., via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim Sefaria English (bold markup removed). About waiving grievances, closely related to not harbouring anger.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One should give up anger, renounce pride, and overcome all fetters. Suffering never befalls him who clings not to mind and body and is detached.”
buddhism.explanation: The opening verse of the Dhammapada's chapter on anger promises freedom from suffering to one who gives up anger and clinging.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the kural, giving up anger leads to the fulfilment one seeks.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verbatim. Reward framed as the absence of suffering rather than the attainment of desires.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Back in his own house in disguise, Odysseus sees the suitors and disloyal maids and is seized with fury, but he strikes his breast and commands his heart to endure, recalling that it endured worse in the Cyclops' cave; this restraint lets him eventually regain his home and family.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus' mastery of rage at the critical moment is what makes his homecoming possible.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Keeping anger from ruling the mind leads to attaining what the heart has long desired, as the kural promises.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. Odysseus defers rather than renounces anger (he later kills the suitors), so the match is partial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Ninth, consider that a good disposition is invincible, if it be genuine, and not an affected smile and acting a part.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus argues that true gentleness cannot be defeated, since the aggressor only harms himself.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the kural, a mind genuinely free of anger is presented as unstoppable in achieving its ends.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim Long translation. 'Invincible' is a close but not identical idea to 'attains all one wishes'.

kurals.tamil:
இறந்தார் இறந்தார் அனையர் சினத்தைத்
துறந்தார் துறந்தார் துணை.
kurals.transliteration:
Irandhaar irandhaar anaiyar sinaththaith
Thurandhaar thurandhaar thunai.
kurals.meaning: Those who go beyond all bounds in anger are no better than the dead. Those who have wholly renounced anger are equal to those who have renounced the world.
kurals.elementary: A person who is always furious is like someone who isn't really alive: there's no joy, kindness, or peace inside. But a person who has given up anger is like a wise holy person. Letting go of anger makes you truly alive.
kurals.university: The closing couplet is a celebrated piece of Tamil wordplay built on two repeated verbs. Irandhaar can mean 'those who have exceeded (all limits)' and 'those who have died'; thurandhaar can mean 'those who have renounced (anger)' and 'those who have renounced (the world)', that is, ascetics. Hence: the excessively angry are like the dead; those who give up anger equal the renunciants. Solomon Pappaiah's gloss offers an alternative reading, that those free of anger are like those who have escaped death, which neatly mirrors the first line. Placed in the Thuravaraviyal (the section on ascetic virtue), the couplet makes giving up anger itself a form of renunciation available to everyone.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who neither hates nor desires the fruits of his activities is known to be always renounced. Such a person, free from all dualities, easily overcomes material bondage and is completely liberated, O mighty-armed Arjuna.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that true renunciation (nitya-sannyasa) is an inner condition, being free of hatred and craving, not an outward vow.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the kural's second line: the person who gives up hostility is equal to the renunciant.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verbatim vedabase. 'Hates' (dveṣṭi) is close to, though broader than, anger.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill ... But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment:”
christianity.explanation: Jesus places anger in the same moral category as killing, linking wrath to the realm of death and judgment.
christianity.tie_back: Like the kural's first line, anger is associated with death itself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verbatim KJV (abridged with ellipsis). Links anger and death; does not address the renunciant half.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, and when they are angry, they forgive,”
islam.explanation: The Quran lists forgiving while angry among the defining qualities of believers devoted to God.
islam.tie_back: Like the kural, letting go of anger is counted among the marks of the spiritually committed.
islam._accuracy_note: Verbatim. Weaker on the 'dead vs. renunciant' contrast; next-best match.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The Sages taught: There are three types of people whose lives are not lives, due to their constant suffering: The compassionate, the hot tempered, and the delicate.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud counts the hot-tempered among those whose lives are 'not lives'.
judaism.tie_back: Almost exactly the kural's first line: the excessively angry are as good as dead.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 113b (William Davidson/Koren-Steinsaltz trans., via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verbatim Sefaria English (bold markup removed). Strong match on the first line only.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who is free from anger, is devout, virtuous, without craving, self-subdued and bears his final body — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: In the chapter on the true brahmin, freedom from anger is listed first among the marks of the holy person.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the kural's second line, being free of anger places one among the renunciant saints.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the close of Aeschylus' Oresteia, the Furies, ancient spirits of vengeful wrath, are persuaded by Athena to give up their rage against Athens and are transformed into honoured guardians, the Eumenides ('Kindly Ones').
greek_mythology.explanation: The trilogy ends with wrath itself being renounced and turned into a blessing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Renouncing anger raises the Furies to a sacred, honoured status, echoing the kural's claim that those who give up anger equal the holy.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase. A mythic, civic transformation rather than individual renunciation; thematic match.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For which reason also, I am not angry with my accusers, or my condemners; they have done me no harm...”
philosophy.explanation: Sentenced to death, Socrates declares that he holds no anger toward those who condemned him.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates facing death without anger embodies the kural's anger-renouncer, who stands above both anger and death.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verbatim Jowett (MIT Classics). A lived example rather than a doctrinal statement.
